item.title: 50 Cent Wins Dismissal Of Ex-Executive’s Lawsuit In Georgia
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: A Georgia judge dismissed Monique Mayers' lawsuit against 50 Cent, and her attorney says she plans to pursue it elsewhere.
item.content:encoded:
50 Cent won the dismissal of his former executive’s harassment lawsuit after a federal judge ruled that the case could not proceed in Georgia.

Monique Mayers can try to bring her claims in another court, and her lawyer says she intends to.

U.S. District Judge Victoria M. Calvert dismissed the case without prejudice on November 18. The ruling addressed the court’s authority over Curtis Jackson and left the merits of Mayers’ allegations undecided.

Mayers argued that 50 Cent had enough ties to Georgia because he signed a 2017 application for G-Unit Film & Television to do business there. The judge found nothing connecting that paperwork to the harassment Mayers says she experienced after her 2019 firing.

“Mr. Jackson’s signature on a corporate registration in 2017 has no comparable link to the harassment that Ms. Mayers alleges,” Calvert wrote.

The judge said G-Unit’s later annual filings were signed by other people.

Mayers also alleged that 50 Cent directed others to send her threatening texts and make harassing calls. Calvert noted that the complaint did not say 50 Cent or anyone acting for him was in Georgia when those calls and messages originated.

“Even taking those allegations as true, the calls and texts were aimed at Ms. Mayers, not at Georgia,” Calvert wrote.

Mayers spent nearly 12 years working across 50 Cent’s businesses.

In the case she filed in April, she alleged that he fired her after she refused to put property in her name or falsely accuse his former bodyguard of theft.

50 Cent’s lawyer Reena Jain previously denied those allegations. In July, his lawyers argued in court that strangers had mistaken Mayers’ phone number for his and that the calls did not establish a basis to sue him in Georgia.

Calvert also denied Mayers’ request to gather more evidence about 50 Cent’s ties to Georgia.

The judge said Mayers hadn’t specified what she wanted that inquiry to uncover. Calvert did allow Mayers’ amended complaint to be placed on the docket.

Mayers’ lawyer, Bennitta Joseph, told Billboard, which first reported the ruling, that her team was “moving swiftly to ensure these serious allegations are heard in the appropriate forum.”

item.title: Becky G Closes Out Record Contract She Signed At 14
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Becky G looks ahead to life outside the contract she signed as a teenager, with a clearer sense of her musical identity.
item.content:encoded:
Becky G is closing out the record contract she signed at 14, describing a new independent chapter after growing up inside the music business.

The singer discussed the change in an interview with Angie Martinez IRL, linking her latest album, Baraja Bendita, to the completion of that deal. She approached the milestone as an artist still deciding what she wants her music to sound like.

“There’s something about the completion of this, this cycle, this contract that I signed when I was 14 years old,” Becky G said.

Her introduction to the industry started with a YouTube cover of Kanye West and Jay-Z’s “Otis.” The performance caught Dr. Luke’s attention, leading to a Kemosabe/RCA deal in 2011.

By 2013, she had released “Becky From The Block” and the Play It Again EP. Her early career was also the subject of an All Def Digital and GRAMMY U interview covered by AllHipHop, when she was still a teenager building an audience through singing, dancing and rapping online.

That catalog grew across languages and styles. Her debut album, Mala Santa, arrived in 2019, followed by Esquemas in 2022, which topped Billboard’s Latin Pop Albums chart. The latter project included her Karol G collaboration “MAMIII.”

Becky told Martinez that experimenting across genres helped her understand both her strengths and the directions that didn’t fit. She singled out her música mexicana album Esquinas as an important step toward finding her own voice.

Her fifth album, Baraja Bendita, brought rap back into focus. During its rollout, she discussed those roots as the music that helped her get discovered, while the project also drew on her experience performing in English and Spanish.

Near the end of the Martinez conversation, Becky described independent artistry as unfamiliar territory and spoke about trusting herself through the transition. She told Martinez she believed her hardest and best work was still ahead of her.

Several of her singles reached No. 1 on Billboard’s Latin Airplay chart, including “Mayores,” “Sin Pijama” and “MAMIII.” RCA Records released Baraja Bendita, and the August album credits list RCA, a division of Sony Music Entertainment. Becky framed what comes next as a change after that album.

item.title: Peter Gunz Invites Fans To Ask Him & Amina Buddafly Anything One Last Time
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Peter Gunz says he'll take questions with ex-wife Amina Buddafly on Dec. 15 after the Love & Hip Hop farewell finale.
item.content:encoded:
Peter Gunz says he’s ready to stop talking about his Love & Hip Hop history with Amina Buddafly.

First, he wants to take questions.

The Bronx rapper announced a live Q&A with his ex-wife for December 15, after the finale of Love & Hip Hop: The Final Chapter.

“This will be my final conversation about this!! So log on and ask us anything. December 15th merry Christmas!!” Gunz wrote on Instagram.

The date lines up with the last of six episodes. VH1 launched the retrospective on November 10 and has been airing it Tuesdays at 8 P.M. Eastern on VH1, BET and MTV. The series uses old footage and new interviews to look back across the New York, Atlanta, Hollywood and Miami shows.

The December 15 finale revisits the franchise’s reunion episodes and looks back at its kids growing up on camera.

Gunz, Buddafly and Tara Wallace became part of that history in 2013.

VH1’s fourth-season announcement introduced Gunz as a rapper managing Buddafly while living with his longtime girlfriend Wallace. Gunz and Buddafly got married, and VH1 showed the fallout as the details of their marriage reached the rest of the cast.

Years later, the cameras were there when Gunz asked Buddafly for a divorce. By 2018, Buddafly was explaining why she filed. The two kept co-parenting after they split, and they’ve both spoken publicly about their relationship since then.

The show introduced Gunz to a TV audience, but he came to it with a hit already behind him. He and Lord Tariq broke through with “Deja Vu (Uptown Baby),” a Bronx anthem that crossed over in 1998. In a recent Drink Champs interview, he talked about the record and the move into reality TV.

He also left the door open to recording with Lord Tariq again, telling the hosts that personal and family issues still needed to be settled. With Buddafly, he’s set a date for what he says will be his last word on their TV history.

item.title: Devin Brown Gets 10 Years In MO3 Killing After Guilty Plea
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Devin Brown pleaded guilty to helping orchestrate MO3's killing and got 10 years, after two other men received life sentences.
item.content:encoded:
Devin Maurice Brown received a 10-year sentence in MO3‘s killing, becoming the last of three men charged in the Dallas rapper’s death to be sentenced.

Brown pleaded guilty to helping orchestrate the killing, and Judge Chika Anyiam accepted the deal, NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth reported.

CBS Texas reported Brown pleaded guilty to murder, a first-degree felony, reduced from capital murder, and admitted to taking Yella Beezy’s payment for MO3’s location.

Brown gave up his right to appeal as part of the agreement. Anyiam said he would have to serve at least half his sentence, NBC 5 reported. Brown had been under indictment since April 2021, months after MO3 was killed.

A witness told investigators that Brown was upset about a relationship involving MO3, whose real name was Melvin Noble. Brown denied being involved when investigators first questioned him.

According to the affidavit described by NBC 5, investigators found calls between Brown and Kewon White the day before the shooting and on the day Noble was killed. They also examined phone location records.

At White’s trial, jurors heard from a woman who had two children with Brown and later dated Noble. She testified that she met Noble in 2017 and stopped speaking to Brown in July 2018. Her testimony brought the relationship described in the affidavit into open court.

The case reached two juries before Brown took his plea.

White, the gunman, was convicted in September and sentenced to life without parole.

At his sentencing, Noble’s mother Nichole addressed White directly: “I love you. Maybe that’s what you needed to hear, and you were looking for love with people that don’t love you.”

Noble was killed on Interstate 35E in Dallas on Nov. 11, 2020. Prosecutors said White followed him from an apartment and chased him on foot along the freeway. The gunfire also wounded a passing driver.

A second jury found Yella Beezy, whose real name is Markies Conway, guilty of capital murder on the sixth anniversary of Noble’s death. Prosecutors argued that Conway hired White to carry out the killing, and the verdict brought a sentence of life without parole.

Conway’s lawyer, Toby Shook, said he planned to appeal and disputed the evidence used to connect his client to the killing. White has also appealed his conviction.

item.title: Doja Cat Bitter Out Rockstar Over GTA VI Snub: “Eat My Dick”
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Doja Cat called out Rockstar Games on launch day and told fans she wanted her music in the new Grand Theft Auto VI.
item.content:encoded:
Doja Cat wanted to hear her music in “Grand Theft Auto VI.” Instead, she spent launch day telling Rockstar Games she wished it had picked one of her tracks.

“I would’ve loved to have my music on gta6 i’m so fuckin bitter,” she wrote on X. In a series of posts.

Even as she cursed out the video game developer, Doja said she loved the game. She’s played the series in front of fans before: in 2021, she streamed “Grand Theft Auto V” on Twitch alongside games including “Fortnite” and “Portal.”

Her music already has a place in another major game. Epic Games featured “Gorgeous” in a Fortnite Festival pass, and “Paint The Town Red” was also available as a playable Jam Track.

The new game arrived November 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Its arrival gave fans two places to look for artists: the music they hear inside the game and the separate album Rockstar released with Atlantic Records.

The 34-track companion album contains new recordings made for the project. Cardi B contributed “Don’t Chart,” and Future and Metro Boomin appear on Yung Lean’s “That’s It.”

The in-game radio works differently. Its stations mix existing songs by genre, and some artists get to pick up the microphone between records. Trick Daddy and Trina host Dirty South Classics, while Robyn and Alex Consani host Flash FM.

As AllHipHop reported, players have already heard Nicki Minaj on Flash FM through Madonna’s “Give Me All Your Luvin’,” which also features M.I.A. That song came out in 2012, years before work on the new game’s rollout went public.

Rockstar’s previews offer a sample of each featured station, so the tracks it has posted publicly don’t account for everything players might hear while driving around Vice City. The game also includes podcasts that players can listen to on foot.

Rockstar will take the music outside Vice City on November 21 with a launch festival in Miami featuring Cardi B, Kodak Black and Metro Boomin.

item.title: Rod Wave Faces Child Support Petition As Process Server Reports Failed Attempts
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: A woman who says Rod Wave fathered her daughter is seeking support. A process server says multiple attempts to serve him failed.
item.content:encoded:
Rod Wave faces a child support petition from a woman who says he’s the father of her daughter.

Azaria Nyla White filed the petition in May, but a process server says repeated attempts to deliver the papers to the rapper have failed, TMZ reported.

White wants the court to set a child support amount and require Rod Wave to maintain health insurance for the child. She also asked for genetic testing if the rapper disputes paternity.

The process server described the unsuccessful attempts in paperwork filed earlier this month. =

The civil filing became public during a separate criminal case in Georgia. A Fulton County grand jury indicted Rod Wave in late October on drug possession, a firearm count and reckless driving.

The charges stem from an Atlanta traffic stop on Nov. 7, 2025. The arresting officer said Rod Wave drove through a stop sign. The rapper was released on an $8,000 bond the next day.

Rod Wave’s lawyers, Marissa Goldberg, Drew Findling and Zack Findling, have challenged that stop and rejected the criminal charges.

“We look forward to vigorously challenging this baseless indictment and the clear violations of Mr. Green’s rights in court,” they told TMZ in a statement about the Georgia case.

item.title: Lil Wayne’s Sports Agency Bosses Up With Brand Partnerships Division
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Young Money APAA Sports picked Brooke Soliz Bremmer to lead a new division handling brand deals for pro and college athletes.
item.content:encoded:
Lil Wayne‘s sports agency has opened a division to find sponsors and endorsement deals for its athletes.

Young Money APAA Sports has named entertainment attorney Brooke Soliz Bremmer to run its new Influencer and Brand Partnerships division.

Bremmer will work out of Los Angeles and report to agency CEO Adie von Gontard. She’ll be the point person for companies looking to work with the agency’s professional and college players.

The agency says it represents more than 100 athletes across football, basketball, soccer and college name, image and likeness deals.

“Young Money APAA has built one of the most exciting rosters in sports, and I’m thrilled to help these athletes turn their influence into lasting brand partnerships,” Bremmer said. “I’ve spent my career on both sides of the camera and the contract. Bringing that together for athletes, brands and the agency felt like the right move at the right time.”

Von Gontard said the hire reflects what companies now ask for: “brands want partners who can tell their stories in a real way.”

Before becoming an attorney, Bremmer worked as a television reporter in Texas and covered entertainment in Dallas and Los Angeles.

She later founded The Zilos Group, a public relations and social media agency. She brings a roster that includes wrestlers, television hosts, actors and online creators.

Wayne and the von Gontard family built the sports agency around a partnership between Young Money and APAA Sports Group.

The companies came together in 2017, according to the agency. Young Money expanded into NFL representation by acquiring PlayersRep Sports Management, adding agents and players to a business that had entered sports through basketball.

The company signed Travis Hunter for NFL playing contracts ahead of the 2025 draft. Jacksonville selected him second overall. In October, Cleveland Browns quarterback Shedeur Sanders hired von Gontard as his first NFL agent, joining his former Colorado teammate at the agency.

The division’s work covers deals outside those playing contracts. On the college side, that includes sponsorships built around an athlete’s name, image and likeness.

The agency had already begun representing college players in that market years before the new division, as its own NIL executive explained to Boardroom in 2023.

For pro clients, Bremmer will pitch brands and manage commercial partnerships alongside the agents who negotiate team contracts.

The agency said Bremmer will also look for projects pairing players with clients from her entertainment roster, which includes digital creator Cam J and actor Matthew Sauvé.

item.title: Pooh Shiesty Moved To Fort Worth After Challenging Jail Conditions
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Pooh Shiesty has been moved to a Fort Worth detention center after challenging his jail conditions ahead of his federal trial.
item.content:encoded:
Pooh Shiesty has been moved from a West Texas jail to a medical detention center in Fort Worth after challenging his conditions in custody, WFAA reported.

He remains in federal custody as he awaits trial on charges tied to the alleged kidnapping and robbery of Gucci Mane.

The move follows a November 10 hearing before U.S. District Judge David Godbey. Prosecutors and defense lawyers agreed to seek another facility and to let the judge know if they could not find one. That agreement did not grant the rapper release.

The Memphis rapper was held at Rolling Plains Regional Jail in Haskell starting in July. His defense said he spent 23 hours a day alone in his cell.

His attorney, Kent Schaffer, also said his client lost about 30 pounds and struggled to sleep.

“It was just mentally wearing him down because he has no contact with people other than through an iPad in short bursts of video visits,” Schaffer told KTXS.

Federal prosecutors disputed the defense’s account of the conditions. FOX 4 reported that they cited more than 12,000 emails and about 230 video calls in their response.

They also argued that the isolation helped protect Pooh Shiesty and keep the jail operating normally.

“It can hardly be said that these conditions of confinement are inhumane, and therefore this emergency motion should be denied outright,” U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould wrote.

Schaffer disputed that rationale. He said Pooh Shiesty had no documented history of violence while incarcerated. He also said the rapper’s family had to make an 18-hour round trip from Memphis for visits limited to an hour.

The charges stem from a January 10 meeting at a Dallas recording studio. Federal prosecutors allege Pooh Shiesty and others held Gucci Mane and his associates at gunpoint.

An FBI affidavit says Pooh Shiesty wanted out of his recording deal with Gucci Mane’s 1017 label and alleges he forced the label owner to sign release paperwork.

Pooh Shiesty has pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors charged eight other men, including the rapper’s father, Lontrell Williams Sr., and fellow Memphis rapper Big30.

The court’s pretrial order sets the trial for the week of February 22, 2027, in Dallas.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Summer Walker’s Team Approved Tour Spending, LVRN Claims As Legal War Gets Nasty
item.dc:creator: Grouchy Greg Watkins (@GrouchyGreg)
item.description: LVRN says Summer Walker's team approved spending on two tours as its amended lawsuit details budgets, staffing and advances.
item.content:encoded:
Summer Walker‘s tour spending was approved by her own team, LVRN alleges in an amended court filing that details its work behind two major concert runs.

The company’s November 19 amended answer and counterclaim, obtained by AllHipHop, says Walker or her representatives signed off on budgets and expenditures for Chris Brown’s 2025 Breezy Bowl tour and her 2026 Still Finally Over It tour.

“In each instance, Walker or her representatives were advised of and approved all tour-related budgets and expenditures,” LVRN states about both tours.

That assertion answers a central part of Walker’s Georgia lawsuit accusing the company of diverting money intended for her career.

She alleged problems involving touring, recording, marketing and merchandise funds, along with concealed financial information.

LVRN’s amended pleading describes the company as responsible for securing her Breezy Bowl opening slot and negotiating her fee. It also claims it handled equipment and rehearsal deals, staffing, tour visuals, on-the-ground logistics and an advance to launch the run.

For the arena tour, the company says it negotiated with Live Nation alongside Walker’s lawyer and WME, arranged Amazon merchandise and helped prepare touring-team agreements.

“LVRN procured and negotiated the tour deal with Live Nation, working alongside Walker’s attorney and her agency, WME,” the filing states.

The company says it also worked with Live Nation on marketing and advanced money for the tour. Those detailed service claims accompany its previously reported demand for seven percent of tour proceeds.

LVRN alleges Walker initially paid its share before stopping in 2026. It seeks damages to be determined at trial, legal expenses and dismissal of her complaint.

Both tours came after LVRN gave up its exclusive rights over touring, merchandising and commercial use of Walker’s name and likeness in a 2021 amendment.

The company also waived its claim to ancillary income owed but unpaid before November 9, 2021.

The revised deal limited LVRN’s share of ancillary income to opportunities it introduced to Walker or her team. That agreement is separate from her Interscope recording contract.

Walker is also pursuing a separate Los Angeles fight with Interscope over video revenue, seeking at least $20 million.

The amended counterclaim remains pending in Fulton County Superior Court.

item.title: Nas-Backed Sweet Chick Shuts Down All Restaurants
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Nas' ties to Sweet Chick stretch back more than a decade as the once-expanding restaurant chain announces its closure.
item.content:encoded:
Nas-backed Sweet Chick is shutting down all its restaurants, ending the chicken-and-waffles business that brought his Queens roots into dining rooms across New York.

The restaurant announced the closures Thursday in a social media statement. Its message thanked customers for their support without identifying a reason for the shutdown.

“After 14 years in business, we’ve made the difficult decision to close all Sweet Chick locations,” the company wrote.

Sweet Chick began in Williamsburg in 2013 before adding restaurants in the Lower East Side, Long Island City, Prospect Heights and Union Square.

Nas joined founder John Seymour’s expansion effort in 2015, when the business was looking beyond its first Brooklyn and Manhattan dining rooms.

For Nas, the Queens opening carried a family connection.

The Long Island City restaurant honored his father, jazz musician Olu Dara, with a hidden back room inspired by Harlem jazz clubs. Nas and Seymour celebrated that opening with relatives, friends and fellow rappers in April 2018.

Seymour described the partnership’s beginnings in an interview with Hypebeast. He had met Joey Bada$$ while opening the original Brooklyn restaurant and later crossed paths with him at SXSW.

Nas arrived as Seymour was discussing the possibility of bringing him into the business.

“We just talked about what we do as a brand, creating a community, building on culture,” Seymour recalled.

Their plans eventually included a different way of serving customers. In 2022, Sweet Chick announced Series A funding from Founders Table Restaurant Group, the company behind Chopt and Dos Toros.

The money was intended to support expansion and finish converting the restaurants to a fast-casual format.

That announcement described Nas as an early investor, while Seymour remained the founder leading the restaurant concept.

The financing came after Sweet Chick had already taken its food and music connections beyond New York, including a Los Angeles location.

Seymour had started changing the service model during the pandemic, according to the company’s announcement, before seeking money for additional restaurant openings.

The brand also collaborated with Clarks Originals on two Wallabee designs, translating its signature meal into caramel waffle and fried-chicken-inspired colors.
